## Introduction ### Overview In these exercises, you'll keep exploring the RNA-seq gene count table from this week's lectures, practicing the R material from weeks 12 and 13 in a few different ways: - In Exercise 1, you'll **predict** the output of code before running it. - In Exercise 2, you'll **find and fix** the mistakes in some code, and see which of them Claude can find. - In Exercise 3, you'll go from a biological question to an answer with _dplyr_, learning two new functions along the way. - In Exercise 4, you'll make and customize a **violin plot**. - In Exercise 5, you'll **recreate** a plot from just an image. - In Exercise 6, you'll use **Claude** to polish a plot and to make a new type of plot, and check its work. - The optional Exercise 7 uses another new function to ask whether a few genes dominate the data. ::: callout-tip #### Lecture page exercises Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture pages that we did not do in class. Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class, go over those again. ::: ### Setting up 1. Open Positron and connect to OSC [like in week 12](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc), and open the `week13` folder that you created in this week's lectures. 2. Create a new Quarto document `week13/w13_exercises.qmd`, with a YAML header with a title, your name, and the date. 3. Add the following code chunk to the top of your document, which loads the tidyverse, reads the three tables from the lectures, and makes a long version of the count table that includes the metadata: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # Read the count table, metadata, and gene annotation table counts <- read_tsv( "/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/salmon.merged.gene_counts_length_scaled.tsv" ) |> select(!gene_name) meta <- read_tsv("../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv") |> mutate(time = factor(time, levels = c("24hpi", "10dpi"))) genes <- read_tsv("/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv") # Make a long-format count table, with the metadata added counts_long <- counts |> pivot_longer(cols = !gene_id, names_to = "sample_id", values_to = "count") |> left_join(meta, by = "sample_id") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: callout-tip #### General tips for the exercises - Install any packages that you haven't installed yet in the console, _not_ in your Quarto document. Apart from installing packages, run all your code in code chunks. - Add a header for each exercise to your document, so it's easy to navigate the rendered document using the table of contents. - Render your document every now and then, to catch problems early. ::: ## Exercise 1: Predict the output For each question, first decide on your answer, and then run the code to check whether you were right. 1. How many rows will this code return? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} meta |> filter(time == "24hpi", treatment != "control") |> nrow() ``` ::: a) 3 b) 7 c) 15 d) 18
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ **b)** is correct: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} meta |> filter(time == "24hpi", treatment != "control") |> nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 7 ``` ::: ::: Because the two conditions are separated by a comma, a row has to meet _both_ of them: these are the 7 _cathemerium_ and _relictum_ samples at 24 hpi. The other answers are 3 (the 24 hpi control samples), 15 (all non-control samples, regardless of time point), and 18 (the rows that meet _either_ condition, which you'd get with `|` instead of a comma).
2. What will this code return? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(counts$S63 > 0) ``` ::: a) The mean count of sample `S63` b) A `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each gene c) The proportion of genes with at least one read in sample `S63` d) An error, because you can't compute the mean of logicals
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ **c)** is correct: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean(counts$S63 > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 0.8318748 ``` ::: ::: The comparison returns a `TRUE` or `FALSE` for each gene, and because `TRUE` counts as 1 and `FALSE` as 0, the mean of these logicals is the proportion of `TRUE`s: 83% of genes were detected in sample `S63`. This is the same as `sum(counts$S63 > 0) / nrow(counts)`, but shorter.
3. First, check how many rows `counts` and `genes` have. Then, predict how many rows each of the following two joins will return: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts |> left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") genes |> left_join(counts, by = "gene_id") ``` ::: a) Both return the number of rows in `counts` b) Both return the number of rows in `genes` c) The first returns the number of rows in `counts`, and the second the number of rows in `genes` d) The first returns the number of rows in `genes`, and the second the number of rows in `counts` Do you know which genes are in one table but not the other? Use `anti_join()`, which is explained on the [optional R self-study page](/bonus/r.qmd#other-types-of-joins), to find out what kind of genes are in `genes` but not in `counts`.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ **c)** is correct: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 18855 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(genes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 19673 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} counts |> left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") |> nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 18855 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} genes |> left_join(counts, by = "gene_id") |> nrow() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 19673 ``` ::: ::: `left_join()` keeps all rows of the first ("left") data frame, adding `NA`s where there is no match in the second one. So the order of the two data frames matters. The genes that are in the annotation table but not in the count table are all pseudogenes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} genes |> anti_join(counts, by = "gene_id") |> count(biotype) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 1 × 2 biotype n 1 pseudogene 842 ``` ::: ::: Conversely, the "unassigned genes" that you saw in the lecture are in the count table but not in the annotation table.
4. How many rows will this code return? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts_long |> summarize(total = sum(count), .by = c(treatment, time)) ``` ::: a) 2 b) 3 c) 6 d) 22
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ **c)** is correct: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts_long |> summarize(total = sum(count), .by = c(treatment, time)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 6 × 3 treatment time total 1 control 24hpi 75446143. 2 cathemerium 24hpi 64139119. 3 relictum 24hpi 88981274. 4 cathemerium 10dpi 80101441. 5 relictum 10dpi 101731001. 6 control 10dpi 61271345. ``` ::: ::: You get one row for each _combination_ of treatment and time point: 3 x 2 = 6.
5. Which of these lines of code return the same result? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mean(counts$S63), 1) round(digits = 1, x = mean(counts$S63)) round(1, mean(counts$S63)) ``` ::: a) All three b) Only the first two c) Only the first and the third d) None
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ **b)** is correct: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(mean(counts$S63), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 1288.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(digits = 1, x = mean(counts$S63)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 1288.6 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(1, mean(counts$S63)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: - In the first line, the arguments are not named, so R matches them by position: first `x`, then `digits`. - In the second line, the arguments are named, so their order doesn't matter. - In the third line, the arguments are not named but in the "wrong" order, so R rounds the number 1 to about 1,289 digits, which is still 1. Note that R doesn't give an error or warning here!
## Exercise 2: Find the bugs The code below is supposed to make a plot of the library sizes of the control samples, with the time points along the x-axis, a box plot for each time point with a different fill color, and the individual samples shown as points on top of the boxes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} control_libs <- counts_long |> filter(treatment = "Control") |> summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = sample_id, time) control_libs |> ggplot(aes(x = time, y = lib_size_M, fill = "time")) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: 1. The code contains five mistakes. Two of these cause an error, but three don't. Find and fix all of them, one by one. For each mistake, note whether it caused an error, and if not, how you noticed it.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} control_libs <- counts_long |> filter(treatment == "control") |> summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = c(sample_id, time)) control_libs |> ggplot(aes(x = time, y = lib_size_M, fill = time)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_point(size = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The two mistakes that cause errors are: - `filter(treatment = "control")` should use `==` to test for equality. The error message even suggests the fix. - `.by = sample_id, time` should be `.by = c(sample_id, time)`. Without `c()`, `time` is no longer part of the `.by` argument, and `summarize()` tries to make a column with all of the values of `time`. The error message (`time must be size 1`) is harder to understand, but it does mention `time`. You probably saw the second error only after you fixed the capital "C" in `"Control"`. That's because the three mistakes below don't cause errors: - `"Control"` should be `"control"`. R is case-sensitive, so no rows match, and `filter()` returns an empty data frame. You might have noticed this from the empty plot, or by looking at `control_libs`. - `fill = "time"` should not have quotes. With quotes, `"time"` is treated as a single fixed value, so both boxes get the same color, and the legend has a single entry: "time". - `geom_point()` should come after `geom_boxplot()`. Layers are drawn in the order you add them, so the filled boxes were drawn over the points, hiding most of them. Mistakes without errors are the most dangerous ones, so always check your output, and not just whether the code ran.
2. Start a new conversation in Claude, paste the original code with the mistakes, and ask Claude to find the mistakes, _without_ telling it what the plot should look like. Which of the five mistakes did it find? Then, also give Claude the description of the intended plot above the code. Which mistakes could Claude only find with this description, or by looking at your data?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ Claude's answers will differ, but it can find the two mistakes that cause errors from the code alone. It may also flag `fill = "time"`, because quoting a column name inside `aes()` is a common mistake. The other two mistakes depend on what you want, and on your data: - Whether `geom_point()` should come after `geom_boxplot()` depends on whether you want the points to be visible on top of the boxes, which is in the description. - Whether `"Control"` is wrong depends on how the treatments are spelled in your data. Claude can only know this if it looks at the data, for example by reading the metadata file, or by running code. So, the more context you give Claude, the more it can check.
## Exercise 3: Vitellogenins In the lecture, you saw that some of the most highly expressed genes are **vitellogenins**: yolk proteins that female mosquitoes produce after a blood meal, to provision their eggs. All mosquitoes in this experiment took a blood meal at the start (with or without _Plasmodium_ parasites, depending on the treatment). In this exercise, you'll see how vitellogenin expression differs between the time points. 1. Find all genes whose `description` in the `genes` table contains "vitellogenin", and save them in a data frame `vg_genes`. How many are there, and on which chromosomes are they? To do this, you need a new function, `str_detect()`, from the tidyverse's _stringr_ package. It checks whether each element of a character vector contains a pattern, and returns a logical: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str_detect(c("vitellogenin-1", "cathepsin B-like"), pattern = "vitellogenin") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] TRUE FALSE ``` ::: ::: Because it returns a logical, you can use it inside `filter()`.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vg_genes <- genes |> filter(str_detect(description, pattern = "vitellogenin")) vg_genes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 9 × 5 gene_id chromosome biotype description transcript_length 1 LOC120420237 chr1 protein_coding putative vitellogeni… 5706 2 LOC128092289 chr2 protein_coding vitellogenin-1 1825 3 LOC120413210 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-1-like 1242 4 LOC120413209 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-1-like 1415 5 LOC120413044 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-A1-like 6445 6 LOC120413042 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-A1-like 6591 7 LOC120428119 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-3-like 1471 8 LOC120426760 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-A1-like 6566 9 LOC120418627 chr3 protein_coding vitellogenin-3 4578 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} vg_genes |> count(chromosome) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 3 × 2 chromosome n 1 chr1 1 2 chr2 1 3 chr3 7 ``` ::: ::: There are 9 vitellogenin genes, 7 of which are on chromosome 3.
2. Compute the total count of all vitellogenin genes for each sample, in millions, and keep the `treatment` and `time` columns in the output. Save the result as `vg_per_sample`. (Hint: recall how you can use `%in%` to [keep rows that match any of several values](w13a_data-wrangling.qmd#filter-to-pick-rows-observations), and that `$` extracts a column from a data frame.)
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vg_per_sample <- counts_long |> filter(gene_id %in% vg_genes$gene_id) |> summarize( vg_count_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = c(sample_id, treatment, time) ) vg_per_sample ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 22 × 4 sample_id treatment time vg_count_M 1 S63 control 24hpi 2.38 2 S64 cathemerium 24hpi 2.05 3 S65 relictum 24hpi 1.80 4 S66 control 24hpi 2.65 5 S67 cathemerium 24hpi 3.75 6 S68 relictum 24hpi 1.57 7 S69 control 24hpi 2.25 8 S70 cathemerium 24hpi 2.97 9 S71 relictum 24hpi 1.99 10 S74 relictum 24hpi 1.58 # ℹ 12 more rows ``` ::: :::
3. Compute the mean of `vg_count_M` for each combination of treatment and time point. Then, make the output easier to read by giving each time point its own column with `pivot_wider()`, which is explained on the [optional R self-study page](/bonus/r.qmd#reshaping-from-long-to-wide-with-pivot_wider).
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vg_per_sample |> summarize(mean_vg_count_M = mean(vg_count_M), .by = c(treatment, time)) |> pivot_wider(names_from = time, values_from = mean_vg_count_M) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 3 × 3 treatment `24hpi` `10dpi` 1 control 2.43 0.00731 2 cathemerium 2.92 0.00830 3 relictum 1.74 0.0130 ``` ::: :::
4. Vitellogenin counts could also differ between samples simply because some samples have larger libraries than others. Compute the _percentage_ of each sample's reads that are from vitellogenin genes. What is the range of these percentages at each time point? (Hint: compute the library sizes like in the lecture, and join them with `vg_per_sample`.)
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lib_sizes <- counts_long |> summarize(lib_size_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = sample_id) vg_pct <- vg_per_sample |> left_join(lib_sizes, by = "sample_id") |> mutate(vg_pct = 100 * vg_count_M / lib_size_M) vg_pct |> summarize(min_pct = min(vg_pct), max_pct = max(vg_pct), .by = time) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 2 × 3 time min_pct max_pct 1 24hpi 7.14 17.4 2 10dpi 0.0388 0.0775 ``` ::: ::: At 24 hpi, 7--17% of all reads in a sample are from just these 9 genes, while at 10 dpi, it is less than 0.1%.
5. How would you explain the difference between the time points? And based on these numbers, would you conclude that infection with _P. relictum_ lowers vitellogenin expression at 24 hpi?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ Vitellogenins are produced in large amounts in the first days after a blood meal, when the mosquito provisions its eggs. At 24 hpi, the mosquitoes are in the middle of this, while 10 days later, it is long over. The _relictum_ samples do have the lowest vitellogenin percentages at 24 hpi: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vg_pct |> filter(time == "24hpi") |> summarize(mean_pct = mean(vg_pct), .by = treatment) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 3 × 2 treatment mean_pct 1 control 9.64 2 cathemerium 13.7 3 relictum 7.88 ``` ::: ::: But with only 3 or 4 samples per group and no statistical test, you can't draw a conclusion from this yet: that's what the differential expression analysis in week 15 is for.
## Exercise 4: Violin plots Is there a difference in expression levels between protein-coding genes and lncRNA genes? A **violin plot**, made with `geom_violin()`, shows the distribution of a numeric variable for each category. It works like a box plot, but shows the full shape of the distribution. 1. Compute the mean count of each gene across all samples, add the gene information from `genes`, and keep only protein-coding and lncRNA genes with a mean count above 0. Save the result as `gene_means`.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means <- counts_long |> summarize(mean_count = mean(count), .by = gene_id) |> left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") |> filter(biotype %in% c("protein_coding", "lncRNA"), mean_count > 0) ``` :::
2. Make a violin plot with `biotype` on the x-axis and `mean_count` on the y-axis. You'll see that the violins are squashed against the x-axis. Why is that? Fix this by adding a `scale_y_log10()` layer, which puts the y-axis on a log scale. And why did we remove genes with a mean count of 0 in the previous step?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A few genes have extremely high counts, so most genes are squashed near 0. This is typical for gene counts, which is why they are usually plotted on a log scale: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin() + scale_y_log10() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The log of 0 is minus infinity, which can't be plotted: _ggplot2_ would remove these genes with a warning.
3. Add the individual genes as jittered points on top of the violins. Because there are so many genes, use the `alpha` and `size` arguments of `geom_jitter()` to make the points semi-transparent and small. Experiment with their values: which work well?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin() + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.5) + scale_y_log10() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: `alpha` ranges from 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (opaque). With a low `alpha`, areas with many points look darker, so you can still see where most genes are. `width = 0.2` reduces how much the points are spread out horizontally.
4. Fill the violins by biotype. Does it matter whether you add this mapping inside `ggplot()` or inside `geom_violin()`? Try both.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.5) + scale_y_log10() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Here, both give the same plot. A global mapping inside `ggplot()` also applies to the points, but the default points have no fill (only a color), so they don't change.
5. Add a narrow box plot inside each violin with `geom_boxplot(width = 0.1)`. What does the violin show that the box plot doesn't? And which of the two biotypes is more highly expressed?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.5) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA) + scale_y_log10() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: (With `outlier.shape = NA`, the box plot's outliers aren't plotted twice.) A box plot only shows a few summary statistics (the median, quartiles, and outliers), while the violin shows the full shape of the distribution. For example, the protein-coding genes have a long "tail" of lowly expressed genes. Protein-coding genes are much more highly expressed than lncRNA genes: note that each step on the log-scale y-axis is a 1,000-fold difference.
6. Finish your plot by adding axis labels, removing the legend, and applying a theme of your choice. Save the plot as an object `violin_plot`, and export it to a PNG file in a `results` folder with `ggsave()`. Finally, in the Markdown text below your plot, write a sentence or two that describes what it shows.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} violin_plot <- gene_means |> ggplot(aes(x = biotype, y = mean_count)) + geom_violin(aes(fill = biotype)) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.05, size = 0.5) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, outlier.shape = NA) + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Gene biotype", y = "Mean count across samples") + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") violin_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE) ggsave(filename = "results/violin_plot.png", plot = violin_plot) ``` :::
## Exercise 5: Recreate this plot 1. Using `vg_per_sample` from Exercise 3, recreate the plot below as closely as you can. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=768} ::: :::
{{< fa lightbulb >}}   _Click for hints_ - The plot has two panels, which you can make with "faceting": see the [optional plotting self-study page](/bonus/r-plotting.qmd#faceting). Look closely at the y-axes of the two panels, and check the help for the faceting function to see how to get that behavior. - The fill colors are `"orange"`, `"grey55"`, and `"skyblue"`. - To remove an axis label, set it to `NULL` in `labs()`.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vg_per_sample |> ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = vg_count_M, fill = treatment)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_point(size = 2) + facet_wrap(vars(time), scales = "free_y") + scale_fill_manual( values = c(cathemerium = "orange", control = "grey55", relictum = "skyblue") ) + labs( title = "Vitellogenin expression is much lower at 10 dpi", x = NULL, y = "Vitellogenin counts (millions)" ) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: The 24 hpi panel comes first because we turned `time` into a factor in the setup code.
2. What does `scales = "free_y"` do, and why is it needed in this plot? What is a downside of using it?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ With `scales = "free_y"`, each panel gets its own y-axis range. Without it, both panels share the same y-axis, and all the 10 dpi values would be squashed at 0, so you couldn't see any differences between the treatments at 10 dpi. The downside is that it's easy to miss that the y-axes differ: at a glance, the two panels look like they have similar values, while those at 10 dpi are hundreds of times lower. (The plot title helps here.)
## Exercise 6: Working with Claude In this exercise, you'll use Claude to go beyond what we covered in the lectures: first to polish a plot, and then to make a type of plot that we haven't covered. 2. Above every line that Claude added or changed, add a short comment that explains what the line does, in your own words. For anything you don't recognize, check the help page, or ask Claude.

3. Did any of Claude's changes affect _which data_ are shown, rather than only how the plot looks? For example, check whether any points or genes were removed, and whether the y-axis now covers a smaller range. Then, edit the code to keep only the changes you agree with.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ In the example above, all changes only affect how the plot looks. One change to watch out for in particular is setting axis limits with `limits = ...` inside a `scale_` function, or with `ylim()`: these _remove_ all data outside the limits (with a warning about "removed rows" that is easy to miss), which also changes the violins and the box plot statistics. To zoom in on part of a plot without removing data, use `coord_cartesian(ylim = ...)` instead.
### A new type of plot 4. Ask Claude to make a plot of `counts_long` that shows the distribution of the gene counts in each of the 22 samples in a single plot, using a type of plot other than a box plot, violin plot, or histogram. If Claude's code uses a package that you don't have yet, install it in the console.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see an example_ Claude may suggest, for example, density curves or a "ridgeline" plot. Here is a ridgeline plot made with the _ggridges_ package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("ggridges") # Run this in the console ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggridges) counts_long |> filter(count > 0) |> ggplot(aes(x = log10(count), y = sample_id, fill = time)) + geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "log10(count)", y = NULL, fill = "Time point") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
5. In the Markdown text below your plot, describe in your own words what the plot shows. Also check how Claude dealt with genes with a count of 0: what did it do, and how does that affect the plot?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ In the example above, each curve shows the distribution of `log10(count)` for one sample, which is very similar for all samples. Claude will typically either remove genes with a count of 0, as in the example, or add 1 to all counts before taking the log, with `log10(count + 1)`. With the first option, the plot only shows genes that were detected in that sample. With the second option, all undetected genes end up at 0 on the x-axis, which adds a peak there. You may also see values below 0 on the x-axis in the example above: these are genes with counts below 1, which are possible because Salmon _estimates_ the counts.
6. Would you choose Claude's plot or violin plots to show these distributions in a paper? And which would you choose to spot a sample that looks very different from the rest? Explain your choices.
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ There is no single right answer here. For 22 samples, a ridgeline plot like the one above is compact and easy to read, and you can quickly spot an odd sample, because all curves are stacked with the same x-axis. Violins can show the same information, but 22 of them side by side get narrow, and if you plot them by time point, you'd need two panels.
## Exercise 7 (optional): Do a few genes dominate? In Exercise 3, you saw that just 9 genes took up about 10% of the reads at 24 hpi. Here, you'll check how much of each sample's reads go to its most highly expressed genes, using another new function: `slice_max()`. It keeps the rows with the highest values in a column --- for example, the 3 genes with the highest counts in sample `S63`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts_long |> filter(sample_id == "S63") |> slice_max(count, n = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 3 × 5 gene_id sample_id count time treatment 1 LOC120426760 S63 1447347. 24hpi control 2 unassigned_gene_22 S63 555170. 24hpi control 3 LOC120413044 S63 537876. 24hpi control ``` ::: ::: Like `summarize()`, `slice_max()` has a `.by` argument to do this separately for each group of rows, but it is called `by`, without the dot. 1. Which gene has the highest count in each sample, and what is its description?
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} counts_long |> slice_max(count, n = 1, by = sample_id) |> left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") |> select(sample_id, time, gene_id, description) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output # A tibble: 22 × 4 sample_id time gene_id description 1 S63 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 2 S64 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 3 S65 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 4 S66 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 5 S67 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 6 S68 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 7 S69 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 8 S70 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 9 S71 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like 10 S74 24hpi LOC120426760 vitellogenin-A1-like # ℹ 12 more rows ``` ::: ::: In all samples at 24 hpi, the top gene is the same vitellogenin gene, and at 10 dpi, it is the unassigned gene `unassigned_gene_22`.
2. Compute the percentage of each sample's reads that go to its 10 most highly expressed genes. Make a horizontal bar graph with one bar per sample, with the bars sorted by this percentage and filled by time point. (Hint: for horizontal bars, put the samples on the y-axis. To sort the bars, see the collapsed box "Sorting bars by value" in the [lecture](w13b_data-viz.qmd#bar-graphs-with-geom_col).)
{{< fa check-circle >}}   _Click to see the solution_ Using `lib_sizes` from Exercise 3: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top10 <- counts_long |> slice_max(count, n = 10, by = sample_id) |> summarize(top10_count_M = sum(count) / 1e6, .by = c(sample_id, time)) |> left_join(lib_sizes, by = "sample_id") |> mutate(top10_pct = 100 * top10_count_M / lib_size_M) top10 |> mutate(sample_id = fct_reorder(sample_id, top10_pct)) |> ggplot(aes(x = top10_pct, y = sample_id, fill = time)) + geom_col() + labs(x = "% of reads from the 10 most highly expressed genes", y = NULL) + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w13_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: At 24 hpi, the top 10 genes take 13--23% of the reads, versus less than 9% at 10 dpi.
